38399: Verses 1-10 and 11-22 are one argument. The same grace that raises individuals from death also creates one new people out of hostile groups. Markus Barth, N. T. Wright and Lynn Cohick stress that for the original readers being 'saved' meant being brought out of their old alienation into God's family with Israel. Salvation has a vertical and a horizontal dimension.
38400: Evangelical scholars such as Harold Hoehner, Peter O'Brien and Clinton Arnold agree that 2:11-22 is essential and that grace creates a community. They also defend the classic point that 2:8-9 speaks of 'works' generally, not just Jewish boundary markers, since it addresses Gentiles who never had the Law; this is often cited against reducing Paul's teaching to ethnic badges. Both sides agree the passage holds personal grace and reconciled community together.
38401: If grace is only personal, a church can be saved yet segregated. Ephesians makes reconciliation across ethnic and cultural hostility part of what salvation is.
38402: 'Wives, submit' (Eph 5:22) read apart from 5:21 and the household code form
38403: Ephesians 5:22-24 sets out the husband's authority and the wife's duty to obey him in everything; this is God's order for marriage.
38404: In Greek verse 22 has no verb; it borrows 'submitting' from verse 21: 'submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ, wives to your husbands'. The household code was a familiar Greco-Roman form that assumed male rule. Ephesians changes it by addressing wives, children and slaves directly, by putting far longer demands on husbands (to love as Christ gave himself up to death) and by calling masters to remember that they have the same Master in heaven (Eph 6:9). Scholars like Lynn Cohick and Craig Keener see this as subverting the code from inside while working within it.
38405: Complementarian scholars (Peter O'Brien, Clinton Arnold, Wayne Grudem) agree that 5:21 governs the passage and that husbands' headship means sacrificial service, not domination. They argue, however, that 'submit' still describes a particular role of wives that is grounded in Christ and the church rather than merely in culture, while slavery is not grounded in creation. Egalitarians reply that the parallel with slavery shows the code is cultural. It is a real scholarly disagreement; both sides reject abusive readings.
38406: This passage has been used both to protect and to harm women. Reading it with 5:21 and the husband's cross-shaped duty rules out domination on every reading. See /debates/gender-roles.
38407: Gentiles who had lived in fear of hostile powers and outside Israel's promises learned that they were seated with Christ above those powers and belonged as full citizens in God's household alongside Jewish believers.
38408: Ephesians speaks to Christians who feel spiritually insecure, to churches fractured by ethnic, racial or class hostility, and to households that need a model of love stronger than mere hierarchy. Its picture of the church as a sign to the powers of God's wisdom (Eph 3:10) gives ordinary congregations a cosmic dignity.
38409: From prison, Paul thanks his most loyal partners and urges citizens of a proud Roman colony to live as citizens of heaven, following a Messiah who gave up status instead of grasping it.
38410: Paul, who founded the church at Philippi with Silas and Timothy around 49-50 (Acts 16), and who received regular financial support from it.
38411: Undisputed. The letter's warmth, personal references to Epaphroditus, Euodia and Syntyche, and its partnership language fit Paul's known relationship with the church, and Polycarp, writing to the Philippians in the early second century, mentions Paul's letters to them.
38413: Paul mentions the 'praetorium' (the imperial guard or a governor's headquarters, Phil 1:13) and greetings from 'Caesar's household' (Phil 4:22), which fit Rome, the traditional view. But both terms could also apply to provincial capitals, and the many journeys between Paul and Philippi (Epaphroditus' trip, news of his illness, planned visits) are easier over the short distance from Ephesus, where some scholars think Paul was imprisoned (compare 2 Cor 11:23). Caesarea (Acts 23:35) is a third option. Coordinates show Rome as the traditional location.
38414: 'All the saints in Christ Jesus at Philippi, with the overseers and deacons'
38416: The church had sent Epaphroditus with a gift; he nearly died and was now returning with this letter (Phil 2:25-30). The believers faced local opposition (Phil 1:28-30), two leading women, Euodia and Syntyche, were at odds (Phil 4:2-3), and Paul warns about teachers who might urge circumcision (Phil 3:2).
38417: Battle of Philippi: Antony and Octavian defeat Brutus and Cassius; veterans are settled and Philippi becomes a Roman colony.
38418: After Actium, Octavian (later Augustus) refounds the colony as Colonia Iulia Augusta Philippensis, with more settlers and Roman legal privileges (approximate date).
38419: Paul, Silas and Timothy found the church; Lydia is baptised; Paul and Silas are beaten and jailed, then released as Roman citizens (Acts 16:11-40).
38420: Date of Philippians if written from an Ephesian imprisonment.
38421: Date of Philippians if written from Roman house arrest.
38422:
Philippi was a small but proud Roman colony in eastern Macedonia, on the Via Egnatia, the Roman highway linking Italy to the East. Its people were very conscious of being Roman: Latin inscriptions dominate the site, its land had 'Italian right' (exemption from some taxes as if it were Italian soil), and many families descended from army veterans. Acts captures the atmosphere: the slave-girl's owners accuse Paul and Silas of 'advocating customs that are not lawful for us as Romans' (Acts 16:21).

Philippi's elite competed for honour through a ladder of civic offices and titles, carefully listed on inscriptions. Joseph Hellerman argues that this 'race for honour' is the backdrop to Paul's description of Christ in Philippians 2:5-11, who descended the ladder from equality with God to slave to crucifixion, and to Paul's own list of credentials that he counts as loss (Phil 3:4-8). Paul also uses political words: 'live as citizens worthy of the gospel' (Phil 1:27, Greek politeuesthe) and 'our citizenship is in heaven, and from it we await a Saviour, the Lord Jesus Christ' (Phil 3:20). In a colony where 'saviour' and 'lord' were imperial titles, this implied a rival allegiance.

The church began with women: Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth from Thyatira and a God-fearer, hosted it (Acts 16:14-15, Acts 16:40). There seems to have been no synagogue, only a 'place of prayer' by the river, so the Jewish community was small. The congregation became Paul's most faithful supporter, giving to him in Thessalonica and Corinth and to the Jerusalem collection out of deep poverty (Phil 4:15-16, 2 Cor 8:1-5). Philippians is in part a thank-you letter, though Paul writes it carefully so as not to sound like a client indebted to patrons.
38424: Colonists were Roman citizens living abroad, governed by Roman law and loyal to the emperor. Paul tells believers in such a city that their true commonwealth is heaven, and they are its outpost.
38426: Elite men advertised their status by listing offices held. Paul lists his own impeccable Jewish credentials and then writes them off, and describes Christ's journey downward to a slave's death.
38428: Greco-Roman friendship involved sharing goods and obligations. Paul calls the Philippians partners in the gospel and receives their gifts as a sacrifice to God, avoiding the patron-client language of debt.
38430: Prisoners depended on friends for food and care, and imprisonment brought shame. Paul reframes his chains as advancing the gospel among the imperial guard.
38432: Stoic philosophers prized being 'self-sufficient', needing nothing outside oneself. Paul uses the word but redefines it: his contentment comes from Christ who strengthens him.
38434: Macedonian women had relatively public roles. Euodia and Syntyche 'struggled together' with Paul in the gospel and were important enough that their disagreement mattered to the whole church.
38435:
Philippians is written to a mostly Gentile church with a small Jewish presence, but Paul's most famous passages are steeped in Israel's Scriptures. The Christ hymn (Phil 2:6-11) ends with every knee bowing and every tongue confessing Jesus as Lord, words taken from Isaiah 45:23, where the one God of Israel declares that every knee shall bow to him alone. Richard Bauckham argues that this places Jesus within the unique identity of Israel's God without abandoning Jewish monotheism. The servant who humbles himself and is exalted also echoes Isaiah's suffering servant (Isa 52:13-53:12).

In chapter 3 Paul gives the only full list of his Jewish credentials: circumcised on the eighth day, of Israel, of Benjamin, a Hebrew of Hebrews, a Pharisee, blameless as to righteousness under the Law (Phil 3:5-6). He does not say he was a guilt-ridden failure; he was, by the standards of his tradition, 'blameless'. What changed was not his assessment of Judaism but his encounter with the Messiah, beside whom everything else became loss. Krister Stendahl used this verse to argue that Paul did not have a troubled conscience before his conversion.

Paul's harsh words, 'look out for the dogs... the mutilation' (Phil 3:2), are aimed at people pressing Gentile believers to be circumcised, probably Jewish-Christian missionaries, not at Jews in general. Reformed readers (Moises Silva, Peter O'Brien) see in Phil 3:9 a clear contrast between 'a righteousness of my own that comes from the law' and 'righteousness from God that depends on faith', evidence for justification by faith alone. New Perspective readers (Dunn, Wright) note that the 'righteousness of my own' is national covenant status ('of Israel, of Benjamin'), not moral self-improvement. Many find both elements in the text.
38437: Paul thanks God for their partnership from the first day and prays their love will abound.
38439: Imprisonment has spread the message; to live is Christ and to die is gain.
38441: Stand together in one spirit and do not fear opponents.
38443: Count others more significant, as Christ emptied himself, became a slave, died on a cross, and was exalted as Lord.
38444: Two living examples of Christ-like concern for others.
38446: Paul gives up his status to know Christ and the power of his resurrection, and presses on to the goal.
38448: Agree in the Lord, rejoice, pray instead of worrying; Paul has learned contentment and thanks them for their gift.
38449: Live as citizens of heaven, with the mind of Christ
38471: Shared life and shared resources in a common cause; used of the Philippians' financial and spiritual participation in Paul's mission.
38473: Appears about 16 times; joy rooted in Christ and the progress of the gospel, not in circumstances.
38475: A way of thinking that shapes behaviour. 'Have this mind among yourselves which is yours in Christ Jesus.'
38477: Christ did not use his divine status for his own advantage but took the form of a slave. Theologians debate what this 'emptying' involved; most say he added humanity rather than subtracted divinity.
38479: To live as a citizen of a city-state; politeuma is a commonwealth or colony of citizens abroad.
38480: Acts 16 describes the founding: Lydia, the slave girl, the jailer and Paul's appeal to Roman citizenship.
38481: The Christ hymn applies to Jesus Isaiah's words that every knee will bow to the LORD, and echoes the servant's humiliation and exaltation.
38482: Paul praises the Macedonian churches, including Philippi, for giving generously in poverty.
38483: Paul came to Thessalonica straight from being shamefully treated in Philippi, and the Philippians sent support there.
38484: Paul's Jewish credentials and his grief over Israel connect Philippians 3 to Romans 9-11.
38485: Philippians 2:6-11 is one of the earliest and highest statements about Jesus. Many scholars think it was an early hymn or poem that Paul quotes; others think Paul wrote it. It moves from Christ's existing 'in the form of God' to his choice to become human and a slave, his obedience to a cross, and God's exaltation of him to receive the name above every name, the divine name, so that all creation confesses him as Lord. For Christian theology this is a foundation of incarnation doctrine. For a Jewish reader it is striking that Isaiah's words about the one God are applied to Jesus 'to the glory of God the Father', which Paul sees as fulfilling, not compromising, Israel's monotheism.
38486: 'I can do all things through Christ' (Phil 4:13) as a promise of success
38487: Philippians 4:13 means that with Christ's strength a believer can achieve any goal: win the game, pass the exam, get the job, overcome any obstacle. It is printed on sports gear and shared before competitions.
38488: The verse comes at the end of Paul's thank-you for a gift. He says he has learned to be content whether well fed or hungry, in plenty or in need (Phil 4:11-12). 'All things' means all these circumstances, including going without. He is borrowing the Stoic ideal of self-sufficiency (autarkeia) and correcting it: his contentment is not inner self-mastery but Christ's strength. Gordon Fee and Markus Bockmuehl read it as 'I can endure anything'.
38489: Evangelical scholars agree almost unanimously with the contextual reading. Some add that Paul's confidence in Christ's enabling is real and can be applied to any faithful task God gives, so it is not wrong to pray for strength in hard work; the error is turning a verse about contentment in need into a promise of winning or getting what we want.
38490: Read properly, the verse supports someone facing poverty, illness or prison rather than promising victory; it can protect believers from feeling that hardship means God has failed them.
38491: Philippians 3 as Paul rejecting Judaism as worthless 'rubbish'
38492: Paul says his Jewish heritage and law-keeping are 'rubbish' (Phil 3:8). Judaism was a religion of works and self-righteousness, and Paul discovered grace when he left it behind.
38493: Paul calls himself 'blameless' under the Law (Phil 3:6), not a failure. He counts his privileges as loss compared with knowing the Messiah, not because they were evil but because they could not compare. Scholars from Stendahl to Pamela Eisenbaum and the Jewish Annotated New Testament stress that Paul writes as a Jew who found Israel's Messiah, not a convert to another religion. His target in 3:2 is pressure on Gentiles to be circumcised.
38494: Traditional scholars such as Moises Silva and Peter O'Brien agree Paul is not attacking Judaism as such, but argue that 3:9 shows he had relied on 'a righteousness of my own that comes from the law', which he now rejects in favour of a righteousness from God through faith; this is the heart of justification by faith. The scholarly disagreement is about what that 'own righteousness' was (moral achievement or covenant status), not about whether Judaism was a religion of grace.
38495: Christian contempt for Judaism has had terrible consequences. This passage can be read as personal testimony about Christ's surpassing worth without disparaging the Jewish people.
38496: A small church in a status-conscious Roman town learned to see Christ's descent, not the race for honour, as the pattern for their life together, to stand firm under pressure and to reconcile their quarrelling leaders.
38497: Philippians speaks to anxiety (Phil 4:6-7), to rivalry and self-promotion in churches and workplaces, and to Christians tempted to give their deepest loyalty to a nation or party. Its joy is not denial of suffering: it was written in chains.
38498: To a young church tempted by a spirituality of rules, visions and angel-worship, Paul says that all the fullness of God lives in Christ, so believers already have everything in him and should live out their new life.
38500: Presented as Paul in prison with Timothy, writing to a church founded by his co-worker Epaphras, a Colossian (Col 1:7, Col 4:12). If not by Paul himself, a close associate, perhaps Timothy, may have written it in Paul's name, during his lifetime or soon after.
38501: The letter claims Paul and ends with his signature (Col 4:18). Its greetings name almost the same people as Philemon, an undisputed letter (Aristarchus, Mark, Epaphras, Luke, Demas, Archippus), and Onesimus is mentioned in both. Doubts arise from style, the cosmic Christology, the teaching that believers are already raised with Christ (Col 3:1), and the household code. James Dunn suggested Timothy wrote it with Paul's approval; Douglas Moo and N. T. Wright accept Paul; many critical scholars do not.
38503: Paul is in chains (Col 4:3, Col 4:18). Rome is traditional; Ephesus, only about 190 km (120 miles) from Colossae, would make it easier for Onesimus to reach Paul and for Paul to plan a visit (Phlm 1:22). Coordinates show Rome.
38504: The mostly Gentile church at Colossae, founded by Epaphras
38505: Colossae, Lycus valley, Phrygia (province of Asia)
38506: Paul had never visited (Col 2:1). Teachers were promoting a 'philosophy' involving food and drink rules, festivals, new moons and Sabbaths, ascetic self-denial, visions, and the 'worship of angels' (Col 2:16-23), implying that faith in Christ needed supplementing. The letter was to be read in Laodicea as well (Col 4:16).
38507: Antiochus III settles about 2,000 Jewish families from Mesopotamia in Lydia and Phrygia (Josephus, Antiquities 12.3.4), the origin of the Lycus valley's Jewish community (approximate date).
38508: The Roman governor Flaccus confiscates Jewish temple-tax money collected in the region, including over 20 pounds of gold at Laodicea, according to Cicero, Pro Flacco 28.
38509: Epaphras evangelises the Lycus valley during Paul's Ephesian ministry (approximate).
38510: A major earthquake strikes Laodicea, reported by Tacitus (Annals 14.27); later writers say Colossae and Hierapolis were also hit. The exact year (60-61 or later) and its effect on Colossae are uncertain.
38511: Traditional date of Colossians and Philemon from Rome.
38512:
Colossae lay in the Lycus valley in Phrygia, in western Turkey, near the larger cities of Laodicea (about 16 km away) and Hierapolis. It had been an important wool town in earlier centuries, famous for a dark red wool dye, but by Paul's day it had been overshadowed by Laodicea. The site has never been excavated; only a mound and surface finds remain, though survey work has begun. An earthquake around 60 damaged the region badly, and Colossae seems to have declined afterwards. If Colossians was written after 61 and the city had been destroyed, it would be odd that the letter does not mention it; this is sometimes used in dating arguments.

The region had a substantial Jewish population, settled there by the Seleucid king Antiochus III. Cicero records that Roman officials seized Jewish temple contributions collected at Laodicea in the 60s BC. Phrygia was also known for intense local religion, including the worship of Cybele and of the god Men, mystery cults with initiation rites, and folk religion that called on angels for protection. Later Christian sources show a strong cult of the archangel Michael at nearby Chonae.

The 'Colossian philosophy' is one of the great puzzles of New Testament study. Paul never defines it; we reconstruct it from his replies. Suggestions include a form of Jewish mysticism in which ascetics fasted to see heavenly visions and join the angels' worship (Fred Francis, Andrew Lincoln), a mixture of Jewish and local Phrygian folk religion (Clinton Arnold), a Greek philosophical school (Troy Martin suggested Cynics), or simply Jewish synagogue teaching about Sabbath and food that attracted Gentile believers (James Dunn). 'Worship of angels' (Col 2:18) could mean worshipping angels or joining in the angels' worship. Whatever it was, it made believers feel incomplete, and Paul replies that they 'have been filled' in Christ (Col 2:10).
38514: People feared 'thrones, dominions, rulers, authorities' and the 'elemental spirits of the world' (stoicheia), which might mean basic principles, the physical elements or the spirits thought to rule them. Colossians says all were created through Christ and disarmed at the cross.
38515: A victorious general paraded defeated enemies through the streets in public shame. Christ 'disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, by triumphing over them' in the cross, turning an instrument of Roman humiliation into a victory parade.
38517: A cheirographon was a handwritten IOU. God cancelled 'the record of debt that stood against us', nailing it to the cross, as if posting the cancelled bill publicly.
38519: Standard teaching on the household addressed the male head about ruling wife, children and slaves. Colossians addresses all members directly and reminds masters that they too have a Master in heaven. Its link with Onesimus and Philemon makes the slavery instructions concrete.
38521: The letter was carried by Tychicus with Onesimus, read to the gathered church, and then exchanged with Laodicea. Christian letters were public documents for communities, not private reading.
38523: To Greeks, 'barbarians' were non-Greek speakers and Scythians, from the Black Sea steppe, were the proverbial savages. Colossians says that in the new humanity these labels give no one a lower rank.
38524:
The great Christ hymn in Colossians 1:15-20 sounds Greek to modern ears, but its background is Jewish Wisdom tradition. In Proverbs 8 Wisdom is beside God at creation, 'the beginning of his ways'. Later Jewish writings such as the Wisdom of Solomon described Wisdom as the image of God's goodness. Colossians says Christ is the 'image of the invisible God', the 'firstborn of all creation' in whom all things were created, and 'the beginning'. N. T. Wright suggests the hymn also plays on the first word of Genesis, bereshit ('in the beginning'), read in Jewish interpretation as 'by Wisdom'. Firstborn here means rank and heir, as Israel and David are called firstborn (Exod 4:22, Ps 89:27), not first created.

Colossians also says believers were circumcised 'with a circumcision made without hands' in Christ's death and baptism (Col 2:11-12), drawing on the prophetic hope of circumcised hearts (Deut 30:6, Jer 4:4). And it calls Sabbaths, new moons and food laws 'a shadow of the things to come; the substance belongs to Christ' (Col 2:16-17).

This last passage needs care. Traditional Protestant readers have taken it to mean that the Sabbath and food laws have been fulfilled and are no longer binding on Christians. 'Paul within Judaism' scholars point out that Colossians is addressed to Gentiles, and its point may be that Gentile believers should not let anyone judge them for not observing these Jewish practices, not that Jews must abandon them. Dunn reads the opponents as local synagogue Jews whose practices were attractive to Gentile believers. Either way, the letter roots its claims in Israel's story: Gentiles have been rescued from darkness and transferred into the kingdom (Col 1:13), language that echoes the exodus.
38526: Paul gives thanks for the faith that came through Epaphras and prays for wisdom and endurance.
38528: Christ is the image of God, creator, head of the church and reconciler of all things through the cross.
38530: Paul suffers for the church and makes known the mystery: Christ in you, the hope of glory.
